summary: William Henry Carmichael Smyth (1780–1861) worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied at Charterhouse School and served as Resident Superintendent at Addiscombe Military Seminary from 1822 to 1824.

William Henry Coxe (1840–1869) was a scholar of linguistics and Indology who studied Classics and Sanskrit at Balliol College, Oxford (1858). He served as an Assistant at the British Museum (1861–1865) and held the unpaid chair of Sanskrit at King's College London (1865).
William Henry Fox Talbot (1800–1877) worked in history, archaeology, and other fields. He completed his education at Harrow School (until 1815) and Trinity College, Cambridge (1817–1821).

William Henry Hale (1840–1919) was an Indology and linguistics scholar. He studied at Yale University, earning a B.A. (~1856–1860) and a Ph.D. (~1861–1863), and obtained an LL.B. from Albany Law School (~1860–1861).

William Henry Harris (1922–1966) worked in philosophy and religious studies. Educated at Southern Nazarene University and Boston University, he studied under T. M. P. Mahadevan at the University of Madras (1953–1954). He held posts at the University of Arkansas and Southern Illinois University Edwardsville.

William Henry Mill (1792–1853) was an Indology and religious studies scholar educated at Trinity College, Cambridge. He served as Principal of Bishop's College, Calcutta (~1820–1838) and later held posts at Cambridge as Christian Advocate (1840) and Regius Professor of Hebrew (1848).

William Henry Sleeman (1788–1856) was an Indology and history/archaeology specialist. He served in the Bengal Army (1809–1854), the East India Company (1820), as General Superintendent of the Thuggee and Dacoity Department (1835), and as Resident at the University of Lucknow (1849–1856).

William Henry Sykes (1790–1872) worked in the fields of Indology and history/archaeology. He founded the Asiatic Society of Mumbai and served as President of the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland in 1858.

William Henry Wait (1854–1939) worked in linguistics and Indology. Educated at Northwestern University, Allegheny College, Humboldt University of Berlin, and the University of Bonn, he held posts at Illinois Wesleyan University and the University of Michigan, where he became Professor of Modern Languages.

William Hoey (1849–1919) was an Indology and history/archaeology scholar who studied at Queen's University Belfast. He served as Reader in Hindustani and Indian History at the University of Oxford (~1906–1913) and at Trinity College Dublin (1910).

William Holme Williams worked in Indology and linguistics. After earning an A.B. at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 1876, he held various posts there, serving as Professor of Hebrew and Sanskrit (1889) and Professor of Semitic Languages and Hellenistic Greek (1892–1917).
William Homan Thorpe (1902–1986) studied at Jesus College, Cambridge (~1921–1925). He taught John Hurrell Crook and held a post at the University of Cambridge from circa 1932 to 1969.

William Hook Morley (1815–1860) was active in Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and history/archaeology. Called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1840, he later served as Librarian for the Royal Asiatic Society of Great Britain and Ireland (1859).

William Howard Campbell (1859–1910) specialized in linguistics and Indology. He studied at the University of Edinburgh (~1876–1882), earning an M.A. and B.D., and served as a missionary with the London Missionary Society from 1884 to 1903.

William Hoyles Drew (1805–1856) was an Indology scholar who studied under the traditional teacher Ramanujan. He served as chaplain of the Madras Chapel for the London Missionary Society from 1834 to 1856.

William Hunter (1755–1812) was an Indologist and linguist educated at the University of Aberdeen. His career included serving as a surgeon at the Agra Residency (~1794–1803), Secretary of The Asiatic Society (1798–1811), and Examiner at Fort William College (1805–1811).

William Irvine (1840–1911) was a scholar in the fields of history, archaeology, and Indology. He studied at King's College London (~1861–1862) and served as a civil servant in the Indian Civil Service from 1864 to 1888.

William J. Gedney (1915–1999) was a linguist who studied at Whitman College and Yale University under Franklin Edgerton. He held posts at Cornell University, the University of Ceylon, and as Professor of Linguistics at the University of Michigan (1960–1981).

William James (1842–1910) was a philosopher and religious studies scholar who studied at Plymouth College and Harvard University. He spent his academic career at Harvard, serving as lecturer, assistant professor of physiology and philosophy, and ultimately as professor from 1885.

Sir William Jones (1746–1794) was an Indologist and linguist educated at Harrow, Oxford, and Middle Temple. He founded The Asiatic Society in 1784 and served as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William in 1783.
